# Lighthouses and buoys (`lighthouse_buoys`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by glass_mirrors, refraction_optics, hydraulic_cement
- Core idea: Mark dangers and harbour entrances so ships can navigate at night and in poor visibility: a tower with a fire or lamps visible from 20–30 km, ideally with a distinctive pattern so each light can be identified, and floating buoys anchored to mark channels and shoals. A lamp behind a polished concave mirror, or better a lens built of concentric glass rings (Fresnel, 1822), sends the light out in a beam many times brighter than a bare flame. Towers on wave-swept rocks need interlocking stone courses set in hydraulic mortar (Smeaton's Eddystone, 1759).
- Pitfalls:
  - Putting the light too low; range depends on height (a 30 m tower is seen about 20 km off at sea level)
  - Identical lights on neighbouring headlands, which leads ships onto the wrong one
  - Unmaintained or unpaid lights; a dark lighthouse is worse than none
- History: egypt: c. 280 BC – Pharos of Alexandria; rome: 1st–2nd c. AD – Tower of Hercules at A Coruña and lights at Ostia and Dover; europe: 1128 – lighthouse at Genoa (rebuilt 1543); c. 1295 buoys in the Guadalquivir to Seville (Compasso da navigare); 1611 Cordouan; 1759 Smeaton's Eddystone; 1823 first Fresnel lens at Cordouan
- Read:
  - D. Alan Stevenson, The World's Lighthouses before 1820 (1959)
